# Acquisition, tracking and signal retention {#sec-tracking-retention}

An estimate from a finite burst can initialize a receiver, but it cannot keep a
local reference aligned indefinitely. Feedback can follow changing phase. It can
also remove the physical phase variation we meant to measure. The engineering
question is therefore not simply how to minimize a detector error: it is how to
retain the wanted signal while controlling nuisance phase and avoiding unsupported
claims about acquisition and recovery.

We use the observation and phase conventions developed in
[Chapters 1–3](observation-weighted-coherence.qmd), and the local/global inference
distinction in [Chapter 5](phase-delay-inference.qmd). No specialist control theory
is presumed. This is a scalar continuous-time teaching model of a phase tracker,
not a complete receiver or a digital synchronization design. Inputs and targets
are illustrative. The mathematical model and local conventions do not establish
hardware performance or book-wide convention authority.

## Build the loop from its physical actions

Let $\theta(t)$ be incoming phase relative to a declared ideal carrier at a receiver
comparison plane, and let $\widehat\theta(t)$ be the local oscillator's correction phase
referred to the same orientation and epoch. Its instantaneous frequency correction
is $\dot{\widehat\theta}/(2\pi)$ in Hz. A phase detector sees their difference plus a
small equivalent input phase error $n(t)$. In a locked, amplitude-valid interval,
normalize the detector's slope to unity and model the correction law as

$$
 \dot{\widehat\theta}=k(\theta+n-\widehat\theta),\qquad k>0.
$$

The gain $k$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$: oscillator integration converts a frequency command
to phase. This is proportional feedback through an ideal oscillator. Actual detector
and actuator gains must multiply to this $k$ after unit conversion. Saturation,
processing delay, oscillator tuning limits, fades and wrapped detector behavior
are omitted for this locked-state model. Define true residual $e=\theta-\widehat\theta$;
the measured detector quantity is $e+n$, which has different noise statistics.

The two output paths in @fig-tracking-loop answer different engineering questions.
The true residual subtracts the oscillator phase; detector noise also enters the
correction and therefore contributes with a negative sign to that residual.
The noisy detector reading includes its own direct noise term.

![Locked-state feedback at one comparison plane. The incoming wanted and nuisance phase share a transfer; the detector reading and true residual differ. All phase variables are radians.](figures/tracking-loop.svg){#fig-tracking-loop fig-alt="Incoming phase and detector noise drive an oscillator correction through negative feedback. The estimate contains positive filtered noise; the true residual contains its negative, while detector output adds the original noise."}

With zero initial conditions, replacing differentiation by the Laplace variable $s$
turns the differential equation into an algebraic equation. Solving gives

$$
 T(s)={k\over s+k},\qquad E(s)=1-T(s)={s\over s+k},
 \quad \widehat\Theta=T(\Theta+N),\qquad e=E\theta-Tn.
$$

Capital symbols denote transforms; the final relation also denotes the corresponding
linear filtering. A perturbation decays as $\exp(-kt)$, so this ideal closed loop is
stable. It has one pole at $-k$ and time constant $1/k$. A phase step $\Delta$ gives
residual $\Delta\exp(-kt)$; a constant phase rate $\Omega$ gives steady residual $\Omega/k$.
These results follow by solving $\dot e+ke=\dot\theta$ with $n=0$. They describe
linear tracking after initialization, not general capture of an unknown carrier.
The small-error replacement of a sinusoidal detector and the separation of input
phase distortion from detector noise are developed in Tausworthe's
[JPL report](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19660008034/downloads/19660008034.pdf),
Part I §§3-C and 5-A. We derive this specific normalization rather than importing
its bandwidth or power conventions.

## Trace the wanted signal before selecting bandwidth

Write $\theta=\theta_s+\theta_d$, where $\theta_s$ is a wanted physical phase variation and
$\theta_d$ is nuisance reference phase. If they enter the same detector input, both
receive the same transfer. In the local oscillator phase estimate they pass through
$T$; in the residual they pass through $E$. A loop cannot infer which part is wanted
from that input alone.

For a sinusoidal phase component at offset frequency $f$, substitute $s=j2\pi f$.
Writing $f_c=k/(2\pi)$, the magnitudes are

$$
 |T|={1\over\sqrt{1+(f/f_c)^2}},\qquad
 |E|={|f|/f_c\over\sqrt{1+(f/f_c)^2}}.
$$

Here $f_c$ is a loop corner frequency, not the RF carrier. As $f$ tends to zero, the
estimate tracks and the residual suppresses the incoming variation. For a sensing
phase variation at 1 Hz and $f_c=100$ Hz, residual amplitude is only 0.0099995 of
its input value. Calling that quiet residual a faithful measurement would remove
about 99 percent of the desired amplitude. The estimate output retains almost all
of it, but also retains low-frequency nuisance phase at that input. Reconstruction
by adding the estimate and true residual is an identity; the available detector
residual includes $n$ and must be interpreted accordingly.

This is an interface decision. A communications receiver may use tracked carrier
phase to derotate a known pilot while retaining information through a separate
modulation-aware path. A phase sensor may need the correction command as part of
its reported observable. Simply choosing the narrowest or widest loop cannot
substitute for identifying where the wanted signal enters and is read out.

## Noise bandwidth and a worked tradeoff

Let $n$ be a centered stationary phase error with two-sided density $S_0$ rad²/Hz on
$|f|\leq B$, zero outside. Assume stable amplitude, linear phase detection and that no
other loop noise is present. The true residual's detector-noise contribution is
$-Tn$, and its variance is

$$
 v_n=\int_{-B}^{B} S_0 {k^2\over k^2+(2\pi f)^2}\,df
 ={S_0k\over\pi}\tan^{-1}\left({2\pi B\over k}\right).
$$

The integral is evaluated by substituting $u=2\pi f/k$. For $B$ much larger than $f_c$,
$v_n$ approaches $S_0k/2$. A locally defined one-sided equivalent noise bandwidth is
$\int_0^\infty|T(j2\pi f)|^2df=k/4$; the two-sided integral is $k/2$. These
are explicit definitions in Hz, not a universal imported PLL bandwidth convention.
White phase noise over an infinite band is an idealized limiting model; the finite
$B$ formulation keeps the observation bandwidth explicit.

Suppose a residual frequency offset of 0.5 Hz remains after coarse acquisition,
so $\Omega=\pi$ rad/s. Let $S_0=10^{-6}$ rad²/Hz and $B=1000$ Hz. The following long-time,
locked-state values exclude initial transients:

| Loop corner | Noise RMS | Steady phase bias | Root mean-square true residual |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 10 Hz | 0.00558712 rad | 0.050000 rad | 0.0503112 rad |
| 100 Hz | 0.0171530 rad | 0.005000 rad | 0.0178669 rad |

The last column is $\sqrt{v_n+(\Omega/k)^2}$, since centered noise adds variance to
the deterministic squared bias. An illustrative 0.02 rad total-RMS target rejects
the narrower loop and admits the wider one under this model. However, the wider
loop strongly suppresses a 1 Hz wanted variation at the residual output. The
receiver decision must consider both error and wanted transfer. Hardware delay,
oscillator noise and saturation could change the feasible choice; none is
validated by this calculation.

The upper panel of @fig-tracking-transfer-budget shows why a small residual may
mean that the wanted phase was suppressed. The lower panel separates stochastic
scatter from constant-rate bias. Only the combined true-residual RMS is compared
with the supplied criterion; the interval does not establish wanted-signal
feasibility without a separate retention requirement.

![First-order phase transfer and finite-band true-residual RMS under the stated locked model. The illustrative 0.02 rad criterion is met for approximately 28.27–134.33 Hz; no wanted-signal retention limit is specified.](figures/tracking-transfer-budget.svg){#fig-tracking-transfer-budget fig-alt="The estimate retains slow input phase while the residual suppresses it. Increasing corner frequency lowers rate bias but admits more detector noise, leaving a bounded range meeting the illustrative residual RMS criterion."}

## Acquisition and nonlinear failure are separate calculations

A useful nonlinear noiseless contrast keeps the sinusoidal detector rather than
replacing it by its slope. For a constant residual frequency $\Omega$,

$$
 \dot e=\Omega-k\sin e.
$$

A stable equilibrium in the principal interval exists for $|\Omega|<k$ at
$\arcsin(\Omega/k)$. Its local slope is $-k\cos(e_{\rm eq})<0$; a companion equilibrium is
unstable. At $|\Omega|>k$ no equilibrium exists and unwrapped error keeps moving,
producing slips. At equality the equilibrium attracts only from one side and gives no robust
operating margin: for $\Omega=k$ and $e=\pi/2+\delta$, $\dot\delta$ is approximately
$k\delta^2/2$, so positive perturbations depart rather than decay. These facts are derived from this specific ideal differential
equation; they are not general capture-range specifications for real PLLs.
Noise, additional poles, delays, limits or detector ambiguities can invalidate a
capture conclusion even when the small-error transfer looks satisfactory.

For our 100 Hz candidate, $\Omega/k=0.005$ and $\arcsin(0.005)$ is close to 0.005 rad.
That consistency supports the small-error approximation for the declared steady
input. It says nothing about starting with an unknown branch or near a fade.
A finite-burst phase/frequency estimate may initialize the oscillator feedforward;
feedback then follows subsequent drift. Feedforward needs its own ambiguity and
staleness assessment, while feedback needs a justified detector domain. Neither
method universally dominates.

A bounded recovery procedure must expose what is known. For this teaching case,
require an amplitude-valid record, an externally resolved phase branch, and a
coarse frequency estimate before enabling linear tracking. Choose illustrative
initial residual $|e_0|\leq0.1$ rad and $|\Omega|/k\leq0.1$. In the noiseless linear model

$$
 e(t)=e_0 e^{-kt}+{\Omega\over k}(1-e^{-kt}).
$$

Waiting $5/k$ reduces the initial-condition contribution to at most 0.000674 rad;
the dynamic bias remains and stochastic excursions are not bounded by that time.
Do not infer a false-lock probability or data-valid flag from this settling
calculation alone. Real validity evidence must include amplitude, innovation,
phase continuity, actuator headroom and an independent ambiguity check appropriate
to the application.

If the reference fades, freeze the last valid frequency command rather than
integrating an invalid detector output. In an illustrative holdover model with
initial phase-error bound $e_{\max}$ and frequency-error bound $\Delta f_{\max}$, the
unwrapped phase-error bound grows as $e_{\max}+2\pi\Delta f_{\max}t$. For $e_{\max}=0.02$ rad,
$\Delta f_{\max}=0.1$ Hz and a 0.1 rad phase limit, holdover is at most 0.127324 $s$ under
constant bounded frequency error. Frequency drift requires another term; unknown
restart phase defeats this continuity argument. After validity returns, repeat
coarse acquisition and ambiguity checks before reenabling the tracker. This is a
bounded interface procedure, not a tested operational acquisition policy.

As a transfer check, place latency $L>0$ in the entire detector-to-oscillator
feedback path. For a perturbation $x$ about a constant-phase equilibrium, the
homogeneous equation is $\dot x(t)=-kx(t-L)$. Trying an exponential mode
$x(t)=\exp(st)$ gives $s+k\exp(-sL)=0$. For an oscillatory mode $s=j\omega$, real and
imaginary parts require $k\cos(\omega L)=0$ and $\omega-k\sin(\omega L)=0$. The first
positive-frequency crossing is $\omega=k$ and $kL=\pi/2$. This is a marginal boundary $L_{\rm crit}=1/(4f_c)$: 25 ms for 10 Hz and 2.5 ms for
100 Hz. Practical margin needs further analysis. The no-delay pole at $-k$ therefore supplies no stability
guarantee for arbitrary latency. Sampled realization, higher-order tracking,
noise-driven slip probabilities and complete system recovery sequences remain
later developments. Preserve the distinction between a locally quiet detector,
a retained physical signal and demonstrated acquisition reliability.


For a reader transfer assessment, replace the constant input phase rate with
$\Omega(t)=\Omega_0+\alpha t$, where $\alpha$ has units rad/s². Retain the same linear
tracker and derive its residual rather than substituting the instantaneous rate
into the constant-offset result. A particular solution is

$$
 e_p(t)={\Omega_0+\alpha t\over k}-{\alpha\over k^2};
 \qquad e(t)=e_p(t)+[e_0-e_p(0)]e^{-kt}.
$$

Substitution into $\dot e+ke=\Omega_0+\alpha t$ verifies both terms. After the transient,
nonzero $\alpha$ makes error grow without bound in the linear model: eventually it
leaves the detector's small-error domain. Waiting longer does not repair dynamic
stress. Identify when a declared small-error limit would be crossed, then revise
the acquisition or tracking model before promising continued lock. During holdover,
a nonnegative bound $\dot f_{\max}$ on the magnitude of the relative frequency-error
derivative, in Hz/$s$, adds $\pi\dot f_{\max}t^2$ to the phase-error
bound. This follows by integrating $2\pi$ times the bounded frequency error. A
constant-offset holdover time cannot be reused unchanged under that new model.

The three panels in @fig-tracking-nonlinear-holdover keep separate the local
equilibrium test, a deterministic holdover bound and a delayed-feedback stability
boundary. None supplies a measured acquisition probability. The
[state and validity sequence](relative-phase-stability.qmd#fig-phase-states)
turns these limits into explicit invalid-data and reacquisition gates; its held-out
fit check and independent validity evidence perform different jobs.

![Sinusoidal-detector equilibria, bounded holdover and the first delayed-feedback marginal crossing. Models are noiseless or deterministically bounded as labeled; hardware capture and practical stability margin remain unverified.](figures/tracking-nonlinear-holdover.svg){#fig-tracking-nonlinear-holdover fig-alt="Below unit normalized rate there are stable and unstable phase equilibria; at equality attraction is only one-sided and above it phase slips. Holdover reaches the 0.1 rad bound at 0.127324 seconds, and marginal latency decreases as one over loop corner."}

# Technical Authoring Standard

**Status:** provisional.

Write primarily for an experienced human RF engineer learning coherent receivers. Each substantial treatment should motivate an engineering question, develop relevant physics and mathematics, define assumptions, interpret results, demonstrate their engineering use, and disclose limitations. Different subjects need different structures: do not impose a mechanical template on all chapters.

- Develop prerequisites or add a targeted mathematical refresher where general RF expertise is insufficient.
- Use complete derivations for essential results; distinguish exact statements from approximations.
- Include system interactions, contrasting architectures and counterexamples where important.
- Use readable diagrams that correctly indicate signal paths, reference planes, directions and units.
- Integrate physical implementation, calibration and verification implications close to the relevant theory.
- Prefer a canonical result with sensible local exposition/cross-reference over copying conflicting derivations.
- Never invent numerical component data or use arbitrary design parameters without labeling them illustrative.
- A chapter's editorial completeness does not imply technical acceptance.

## Pilot-tested minimum obligations (2026-10-29; human acceptance pending)

For each consequential result supply the observable, reference planes, observation
operator, state, calibration history, physical model and stochastic assumptions.
Define symbols and units before use. Develop indispensable steps internally;
identify exact identities, modeling choices and approximations separately. Check
dimensions, limiting cases and error scales. A covariance is constructed from
physical sources and paths, not chosen merely to obtain a favorable budget.

Keep instantaneous phase variance, increments, calibrated residuals, restart
statistics and application performance distinct. Averaging phase and taking the
phase of an averaged complex product are different operations. Every integral
needs its spectral domain and convergence conditions. Preserve endpoint transfer
functions until a justified reduction is made.

A numerical example exposes inputs and their provenance, intermediate results,
uncertainty, decision and rejected alternative without requiring code execution.
Include a diagnostic counterexample and a transfer question that changes the
model. A design recommendation includes interface, implementation, calibration
access and evidence consequences. Introduce specialist mathematics in the reading
path from the RF baseline; a source citation cannot replace the bridge.

Keep general derivations in one home. The relative-phase pilot temporarily owns
its general results; its brief records their eventual chapter destinations.

## Integration of bounded units

Write a continuous learning argument rather than exposing the task template in
the manuscript. Keep project codes and review metadata in supporting records.
Name a canonical destination; supply local prerequisite and applicability bridges,
and review the surrounding chapter progression when integrating a unit. Transfer
pilot results only in a bounded migration that updates references and assesses
the affected acceptance scope. Until then, introductory restatements identify
their scope and do not supersede the pilot's general derivations.

## Visual reasoning alongside the derivation

For each consequential explanation, assess whether a graphic improves physical
interpretation, transfer or error prevention. Specify its teaching purpose, source
model and assumptions before drawing; justify no-figure decisions where needed.
Use shared canonical figures and local interpretation instead of redundant copies.
Introduce and interpret each figure in the argument. Declare synthetic inputs,
axes/units, normalizations, reference planes and failure regions; provide meaningful
alt text and a caption that explains what the reader should learn. Preserve
reproducible generating equations, parameters and editable assets. No figure quota.
# Verification and Acceptance Standard

**Status:** provisional.

## What evidence establishes
- Algebraic/symbolic checks support mathematical consistency under encoded assumptions.
- Unit tests support implementation correctness for tested cases.
- Limiting cases, independent derivations, reference comparisons and convergence checks broaden confidence but do not automatically validate physics.
- Physical validation requires representative empirical evidence with stated domain and uncertainty.
- Requirements compliance is specific to the implemented system and its specified conditions.

## Risk-proportionate review
Use stronger independent methods for consequential system budgets, synchronization promises, phase-noise models, calibration identifiability and acceptance criteria. Do not treat repeated AI reasoning as independent physical evidence.

## Technical states
- **Draft:** unaccepted material.
- **Checked:** specific mechanical/mathematical/computational checks recorded.
- **Reviewed:** an engineer examined relevant reasoning and limitations.
- **Accepted for stated use:** human decision backed by adequate evidence; may later be restricted or superseded.
These labels are not identical to evidence type or publication readiness.

## Minimum acceptance information
Claim and intended use, assumptions, evidence/checks executed, important uncertainties, blocking issues, reviewing engineer and date/revision if formally accepted. Never fabricate a review record or claim human acceptance.

## Pilot checks and educational assessment

For consequential calculations compare distinct formulations, appropriate limits,
units, convergence and sampling error. A seeded simulation is reproducible, not
independent physical evidence. Code and analytical formulas sharing an assumption
cannot validate that assumption. Record unavailable dependencies and failed
commands as well as successful checks.

A reader assessment requires an actual RF-engineer participant to define a
measurand, calculate a decision, reject a misleading result, change the model for
a new topology/observation, and find applicability conditions. Record assistance,
reasoning errors and revisions; a small trial cannot establish general learning
effectiveness. A critical reference/sign/correlation/observability error requires
revision and reassessment. Authorial self-check is not specialist review.

Final human acceptance states separately: planning suitability; mathematical
correctness under assumptions; physical applicability; educational/practical
adequacy; experimental confirmation; and compliance for a named implementation.
Missing review or empirical evidence remains pending rather than inferred.

## Review of connections and task closure

Challenge the connections between observable, physical model, calculation,
implementation/procedure and evidence, not just the individual formulas. Use
asymmetric inputs or changed references/operators where symmetry can hide a defect.
Record correction propagation to dependent results and repeat affected checks.
A bounded task may close as a completed, checked provisional draft with human
review pending; this is distinct from human technical acceptance and publication
integration. Assess physical applicability separately; theoretical identities do
not universally require laboratory tests, while hardware-performance claims need
representative evidence. Publication integration additionally needs reading-path,
notation, cross-reference and rendered-presentation review for the intended edition.

## Separate-context AI review

AI review is additional evidence, not the human **Reviewed** state. Use a fresh
conversation with no author history or correctness assertions. Freeze input bytes
and record SHA-256 when HEAD does not identify them. Give the reviewer accepted
requirements, manuscript, applicable standards and actual source access; inspect
reasoning before author check code. Seek alternative derivations, limiting cases,
asymmetric counterexamples and failures of assumptions, reference planes and
engineering interpretation.

Classify findings as demonstrated errors, model/applicability concerns, missing
evidence, pedagogical defects or optional improvements. Record location, consequence,
evidence, author disposition, correction propagation and reassessment. Identify AI
model/effort/session, sources actually examined, checks run and unperformed checks.
A separate context using the same model retains correlated failure risks. Review
failure blocks progression; unavailable evidence restricts dependent claims.

## Visual-adequacy gate for bounded teaching units

Assess scientific correctness and pedagogical communication separately. Check
quantitative curves through independent formulations, limits and spot values;
check schematic paths, signs, planes and correlation against the model. Follow
[the actual-image procedure](../docs/VISUAL-INSPECTION.md): inspect standalone pixels
and the complete rendered page with readable detail crops, equations and captions.
Fresh read-only AI review receives actual raster attachments and frozen models;
record image access, readability limits, findings and correction reassessment.
Source parsing, successful capture and render success alone never clear this gate.

A missing indispensable explanation, consequential model/graphical error, unreadable
figure, failed image inspection or unresolved consequential review finding blocks
a positive visual-adequacy recommendation. Optional polish can remain documented.
AI visual review does not grant human acceptance, reader-trial evidence or physical
validation, and does not authorize subsequent canonical authoring.
# Notation and Conventions

**Status:** initial proposal; canonical conventions must be reviewed before substantive mathematical chapters.

## Proposed conventions to confirm
- Continuous-time Fourier transform: `X(f) = ∫ x(t) exp(-j 2π f t) dt` and inverse with `+j 2π f t`.
- Angular frequency `ω = 2π f`, frequency `f` in hertz.
- Real physical waveforms vs complex analytical signals/envelopes must carry explicit scaling and carrier-sign conventions.
- Unwrapped phase and circular/angle-valued statistics are distinct; specify the one used.
- Spectral densities: explicitly state one-/two-sided definition, variable, units, domain and cross-spectrum ordering.
- Time and phase reference planes, trigger/reset state, bandwidth/filter and observation interval must accompany consequential phase measures.
- Clearly distinguish power and amplitude ratios in dB, and RMS vs peak conventions.

## Unresolved choices
General complex-envelope normalization, default PSD convention, phase-noise `L(f)` normalization, cross-spectrum sign/order, treatment of distributional/nonstationary spectra. Do **not** silently resolve these by defaulting to whatever an external source uses.

## Relative-phase pilot conventions (local selection; review pending)

These explicit local choices permit a reviewable draft; they are not accepted
book-wide defaults. Human mathematical/engineering review remains outstanding.

- `v(t)=Re{z(t) exp(j 2π fc t)}`; z has peak-voltage scaling. For a constant
  envelope into a declared resistance R, power is `|z|²/(2R)`.
- Relative phase is channel 2 relative to 1: `arg(z2 conj(z1))`.
- Use the proposed Fourier pair above. Define centered correlation
  `Rxy(τ)=E[(x(t+τ)-μx) conj(y(t)-μy)]` and its transform `Sxy`.
  Thus `Sxy` corresponds to `X conj(Y)` and `Syx=conj(Sxy)`.
- Derivations use two-sided spectra over all real offset frequencies, in
  rad²/Hz for phase. State band limits explicitly. Imported one-sided spectra
  require an explicit conversion; no universal L(f) conversion is selected.
- A physical delay has transfer `exp(-j 2π f τ)`; group delay is the negative
  phase derivative with respect to angular frequency. State RF versus offset f.
- Unwrapped residuals require continuity and amplitude/SNR conditions; otherwise
  use circular quantities and report slips, gaps and invalid intervals.
- Noise spectra describe centered processes. Deterministic drift, spurs and

## Start with a decision {#sec-phase-problem}

Two nominally identical receivers compare the phase of a tone at 1 GHz. Should
they distribute one LO, or synthesize two LOs locked to one frequency reference?
The useful answer depends on endpoint paths, observation time and what must
remain repeatable after a restart. Sharing a source does not remove everything
added after the split. A quiet display can also conceal a bad test reference.

Our teaching requirement is a band-selected continuous relative-phase standard
deviation below 1.5 degrees, plus no more than 0.5 degree deterministic drift
between calibrations. These are illustrative, separate limits; they are not a
customer specification or a universal coherence criterion. Restart behavior is
reported separately, without an invented repeatability limit. For each declared
event j define $r_j=\arg[\int_{5\,s}^{5.01\,s}p_j(t)dt]$, time zero being
that event, after its own valid-state checks. This 10 ms circular observation
samples restart repeatability; failed settling by 5 s is an invalid event, not an
omitted outlier. Use separate distributions for cold start, warm reset and retune.
The arbitrary 5 s teaching interval is not a hardware settling guarantee. Later we derive
what the same disturbances mean for a particular coherent combination.

Use two colocated heterodyne channels, a common 1 GHz calibration tone, fixed
gain and adequate signal level without overload. Choose the lower-side LO so
that the ideal difference-frequency complex signal retains RF phase and
subtracts LO phase. At an amplitude null phase is undefined. Reject such records;
do not manufacture a phase by unwrapping noise. No antenna, propagation inference,
wideband equalizer, converter selection or full PLL design is included.

![Reference planes and two possible endpoint reference paths. RF fixture paths remain nuisance terms until characterized.](figures/relative-phase-reference-planes.svg){#fig-phase-planes}

The input planes P1/P2 are the RF connectors; L1/L2 are the LO mixer inputs;
O1/O2 are complex receiver outputs before correction, after acquisition and

before acquisition (not separately drawn in @fig-phase-planes). Acquisition

## Representations and the first physical model {#sec-phase-model}

Write a physical voltage as

$$v_i(t)=\operatorname{Re}\{z_i(t)e^{j2\pi f_c t}\}.$$

The envelope has peak-voltage scaling. Constant-envelope power into a stated
resistance R is $|z_i|^2/(2R)$; the envelope is not automatically power-normalized.
After ideal difference conversion and removal of the nominal IF rotation, use

$$z_i(t)=A_i(t)e^{j[\psi_i(t)-\ell_i(t)+\beta_i(t,q)]}+n_i(t).$$ {#eq-channel}

Here $\psi_i$ is the input phase at Pi, $\ell_i$ the LO endpoint phase at Li,
$\beta_i$ the remaining conversion/output phase, and q the operating state.
This is a narrowband model: approximately constant channel response across the
stimulus bandwidth, adequate isolation, negligible compression and image response.
Those are applicability assumptions, not conclusions from the computations.
A positive RF path delay contributes $-2\pi f_c\tau$; spectral inversion or an
opposite mixing side requires rederiving the sign in @eq-channel.

For nonzero signal amplitudes,

$$p(t)=z_2(t)z_1^*(t),\qquad \theta(t)=\arg p(t).$$

Without additive noise, the unwrapped relative phase is

$$\theta=\psi_2-\psi_1-(\ell_2-\ell_1)+(\beta_2-\beta_1).$$ {#eq-relative}

The desired input difference and receiver error are different unknowns. A common
calibration source does not establish equal input phase: its splitter and cables
create $\psi_2-\psi_1$. Receiver delay and fixture delay are confounded unless
another observation or characterization separates them.

For a signal phasor $Ae^{j\alpha}$, rotate the additive noise by $e^{-j\alpha}$:
$\arg(A+n')=\operatorname{atan2}(\operatorname{Im}n',A+\operatorname{Re}n')$
for $A+n'\ne0$; phase is undefined at zero amplitude.
Expanding at $n'=0$ gives phase error $\eta\simeq\operatorname{Im}n'/A$.
Thus differential phase noise includes $\eta_2-\eta_1$, with covariance retained.
This approximation fails for fades, low SNR, appreciable AM/PM conversion and slips;
it does not imply Gaussian, white or independent noise.

A useful decomposition is $\theta(t)=d(t,q)+x(t)$ within a valid fixed state.
The deterministic part includes a phase intercept, $2\pi\Delta\nu t$, RF delay
change and deterministic supply/temperature response. The centered random part
contains explicitly filtered physical sources. State transitions need a separate
model; a random restart intercept is not stationary within-run noise.

## A short probability and spectral bridge {#sec-phase-statistics}

Expectation averages hypothetical repetitions under the model. Variance measures
squared deviations from that ensemble mean. Covariance tells whether deviations
in two quantities occur together. For real variables,
$\operatorname{var}(aX+bY)=a^2\operatorname{var}X+b^2\operatorname{var}Y+
2ab\operatorname{cov}(X,Y)$: expand the squared centered sum to obtain it.
Positive correlation therefore reduces a difference but increases a sum.
An observed time average estimates an ensemble quantity only under suitable
sampling and ergodic assumptions; a long record alone does not establish them.

For centered, jointly wide-sense stationary processes define

$$R_{ij}(\tau)=E[x_i(t+\tau)x_j^*(t)],\quad
S_{ij}(f)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}R_{ij}(\tau)e^{-j2\pi f\tau}\,d\tau.$$

Here f is offset frequency in Hz. The spectra are two-sided; phase PSD has units
rad²/Hz. The inverse transform uses the positive exponential. We assume the
integrals exist in the usual sense for the examples, rather than quietly using
a generalized PSD for an unbounded random walk.

Let $y_i=g_i*x_i$. Substituting both convolutions into the correlation, the lag
argument becomes $\tau-u+v$. Its Fourier transform yields
$S_{y_i y_j}=G_i S_{ij}G_j^*$. Therefore a linear combination with row vector h has

$$S_y=\sum_{ij}h_i S_{ij}h_j^*=\mathbf h\mathbf S\mathbf h^H.$$ {#eq-spectral}

A covariance/spectral matrix is Hermitian and positive semidefinite: for every
h, this variance or spectrum must be nonnegative. For a Hermitian two-by-two
matrix, nonnegative diagonal entries together with $|S_{12}|^2\le S_{11}S_{22}$
are necessary and sufficient for positive semidefiniteness. For larger matrices
pairwise bounds are only necessary: a three-by-three matrix with unit diagonal
and every off-diagonal entry -0.9 satisfies every pairwise bound but has eigenvalue
-0.8 along (1,1,1). Full positive semidefiniteness is required at each f, with
conjugate frequency symmetry for real processes and convergence of the relevant
observation integrals. These are mathematical admissibility conditions, not
evidence that hardware realizes the spectra. Complex cross-spectral phase
matters; replacing it with a real correlation coefficient can lose delay effects.

For two endpoints, write $\ell_i=G_i*r+v_i$ in phase perturbations. Then

$$S_{\Delta\ell}=|G_2-G_1|^2S_r+S_{v_2}+S_{v_1}
 -2\operatorname{Re}S_{v_2v_1}
 +2\operatorname{Re}\{(G_2-G_1)S_{r,v_2-v_1}\}.$$ {#eq-endpoints}

The last term disappears only with justified uncorrelated reference and branch
processes. Include the remaining receiver/input/measurement disturbances through
@eq-spectral rather than adding unconditional RMS numbers. Transfer functions
may be complex, dispersive and state dependent. They are phase-disturbance
responses around a valid operating point, not simply carrier insertion phase.

If both branches really are pure delays, their difference magnitude squared is
$4\sin^2(\pi f\Delta\tau)$. Factor out their common exponential and multiply by
the conjugate to obtain this identity. Only for $|\pi f\Delta\tau|\ll1$ may it be
replaced by $(2\pi f\Delta\tau)^2$; the relative leading error is approximately
$(\pi f\Delta\tau)^2/3$. Equal delays cancel that common source, not additive
branch noise. Equal cable lengths do not establish equal endpoint responses.

Phase deviation, frequency deviation and positive time advance satisfy
$\delta\nu=\dot\phi/(2\pi)$ and $a=\phi/(2\pi f_c)$. Where differentiable
stationary spectra are meaningful, $S_{\delta\nu}=f^2S_\phi$ and
$S_a=S_\phi/(2\pi f_c)^2$. Physical delay has the opposite phase sign.
No oscillator single-sideband L(f) conversion is needed here.

## Which statistic did the requirement mean? {#sec-phase-observation}

Let $x$ be the centered real unwrapped residual at O2 relative to O1 in a fixed
state, with deterministic terms reported separately. Define a normalized phase
observation $a(t)=\int w(u)x(t+u)du$; its transfer magnitude is $|W(f)|$.
For a rectangular average of duration T, it is $|\operatorname{sinc}(fT)|$,
where $\operatorname{sinc}(u)=\sin(\pi u)/(\pi u)$. Expansion of the double
integral of the covariance gives

$$\operatorname{var}a=\iint w(u)w(v)R_x(u-v)du\,dv
 =\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}S_x(f)|W(f)|^2df.$$ {#eq-observe}

These equalities require second-order stationarity and convergent integrals,
not Gaussianity. Here W acts on an **already extracted phase process**.
A phase-domain filter B may be cascaded by including $|B|^2$.
An analog or complex-signal filter cannot generally be inserted this way.

For a bounded small-perturbation bridge, write a derotated complex signal as
$z=A(1+\alpha+j\phi)+n$, with real small amplitude perturbation alpha and small
phase phi around a nonzero constant carrier. A complex baseband filter with
impulse response h has carrier gain $H_0=\int h(u)du\ne0$. Divide its output
by $AH_0$ and expand the argument at unity:

$$\phi_{\rm out}\simeq
 \operatorname{Im}\{(h/H_0)*(\alpha+j\phi+n/A)\}
 =\operatorname{Im}(h/H_0)*\alpha+
 \operatorname{Re}(h/H_0)*\phi+
 \operatorname{Im}\{(h/H_0)*n/A\}.$$

The real and imaginary parts here are of the *impulse response*. Only if its
normalized imaginary part vanishes does pure phase transfer reduce to that real
impulse response without AM-to-PM coupling. Both sidebands, additive-noise
quadratures and correlations can matter. For an analog IF filter first translate
its response about the carrier to obtain h; a carrier notch ($H_0=0$), large
excursions or fades invalidate this expansion. Ideal B below is post-extraction
phase filtering, not an analog or complex channel filter. Acquisition antialias
and digital channel filters precede extraction and need their own noise/image/
alias model. Quantitative alias, quantization and blocker/AM-to-PM budgets are
omitted; predictions assume them negligible or separately allocated.

These are observation predictions; a finite sample variance is an estimator with
its own uncertainty.

| Quantity | Precise operator and interpretation |
|---|---|
| Instantaneous variance | $R_x(0)=\int S_xdf$ of the declared process, or filtered process; may not exist |
| Increment at lag L | $x(t+L)-x(t)$; variance $2[R_x(0)-R_x(L)]=\int4\sin^2(\pi fL)S_xdf$ for real stationary x |
| Calibration residual | observation now minus observation at calibration epoch; includes their covariance and calibration error |
| Restart repeatability | distribution across specified independent restarts of a fixed post-settling circular-phase observation; retain between-run offsets |
| Coherent performance | functional of complex samples and application weights; derive below |

For two rectangular phase averages whose centers are separated by L, stationary
residual variance is $\int S_x|W_T|^2 4\sin^2(\pi fL)df$. Add calibration
estimation/fixture uncertainty and cross-covariance explicitly. Calling this
$2\operatorname{var}a$ assumes negligible correlation between the two averages.
In sampled form any linear phase statistic has variance
$\sum_{ij}w_iw_jR_x(t_i-t_j)$ and spectral gain
$|\sum_iw_i e^{j2\pi ft_i}|^2$; the supporting calculation compares these forms.

Subtracting a fitted slope/intercept from one finite record is another operator,
a projection depending on that record. It is not a universal high-pass filter,
and the reduced residual does not show that drift disappeared physically.
The choice of stability statistic matters for divergent clock noise
[@riley2008frequency, sec. 5.2.1]; we do not apply the stationary integrals above
to such noise merely by choosing a convenient low-frequency cutoff.

As a checkable process example, choose $R_x(\tau)=\sigma^2e^{-|\tau|/t_c}$.
Integrating its positive and negative lags gives
$S_x(f)=2\sigma^2t_c/[1+(2\pi ft_c)^2]$. The increment variance is
$2\sigma^2(1-e^{-L/t_c})$: zero at L=0 and twice the marginal variance at
large L. This covariance does not itself establish Gaussianity. A stationary
Gaussian realization sampled at spacing h can be generated by
$x_{k+1}=\rho x_k+\epsilon_k$, $\rho=e^{-h/t_c}$, with independent Gaussian
innovations of variance $\sigma^2(1-\rho^2)$ and stationary initial variance.
A random walk instead has increment variance proportional to L while its
absolute variance depends on start time. A deterministic spur must be propagated
as a waveform (or with an explicitly randomized phase), not silently mixed into
a smooth noise density.

## From phase to an engineering consequence {#sec-phase-combination}

For equal-amplitude, aligned channels, normalize their instantaneous combination
to ideal output power: $P(t)=|1+e^{j e(t)}|^2/4=[1+\cos e(t)]/2$.
Here e is the actual differential phase at the combiner, including calibration
bias. For a Gaussian real residual with mean b and variance v at that instant,

$$E[P]=(1+\cos b\,e^{-v/2})/2.$$ {#eq-combine}

To derive the Gaussian factor without a small-angle argument, let
$F(a)=E[e^{ja(x-b)}]$. The centered normal density g satisfies
$g'(u)=-ug(u)/v$. Differentiate F under the integral and integrate by parts;
the Gaussian boundary term vanishes and $F'(a)=-vaF(a)$. With $F(0)=1$, this
gives $F(a)=e^{-va^2/2}$ and $E[e^{jx}]=e^{jb-v/2}$. This is exact under Gaussianity,
without a small-angle expansion. Other distributions require their own
characteristic function. For small b and v the loss is approximately
$(b^2+v)/4$. Unequal amplitudes change the normalization and weighting.
The 1–10000 Hz filtered statistic used below predicts this physical combination
only if that is also the residual process at its input, or omitted contributions
are separately included. Measurement filtering does not remove physical errors.

Temporal coherent accumulation is a different question. For normalized real
weights $\sum w_k=1$, define $C=\sum w_ke^{je_k}$. Its mean complex amplitude is
$E[C]=\sum w_k E[e^{je_k}]$, but

$$E|C|^2=\sum_{kl}w_kw_l E[e^{j(e_k-e_l)}].$$ {#eq-accumulation}

For jointly Gaussian stationary centered e, the last expectation is
$\exp[-(R(0)-R(t_k-t_l))]$. This follows by applying the same Gaussian integral
to the increment whose variance is $2(R(0)-R(\tau))$. With deterministic phase,
multiply each term by $e^{j(d_k-d_l)}$. Without Gaussianity, second moments alone
cannot determine it.

A phase that is Gaussian but frozen during each record has marginal variance
$\sigma^2$, $|E[C]|^2=e^{-\sigma^2}$, yet $E|C|^2=1$.
Independent Gaussian phase samples of the same variance give
$E|C|^2=1/N+(1-1/N)e^{-\sigma^2}$ for equal weights. Equal marginal RMS phase
therefore does not specify temporal coherent performance. Neither example
establishes a radar, array or communications performance guarantee.

Finite-record uncertainty also needs temporal structure. If $\hat m=N^{-1}
\sum Y_k$, expand its variance to get
$\operatorname{var}\hat m=N^{-2}\sum_{ij}\operatorname{cov}(Y_i,Y_j)$.
For equal marginal variance $\sigma_Y^2$, this equals
$\sigma_Y^2/N+(2/N^2)\sum_{i<j}\operatorname{cov}(Y_i,Y_j)$.
Independence is sufficient but unnecessary: a zero *sum* of off-diagonal
covariances gives the usual result, including pairwise uncorrelated dependent
samples or cancelling nonzero covariances. Negative or positive sums can reduce
or increase it. Aggregate covariance determines the approximation. For nonlinear power
statistics, these covariances generally require fourth moments or a justified
full distribution. The tests use independent simulated records to estimate
Monte Carlo standard error; they do not count correlated samples as repetitions.

The measured phase is referred from Pi to the selected Oi channelizer output,
including IF/acquisition response unless de-embedded. At fixed LO an RF sweep
changes IF by the same increment. For nondispersive differential RF, IF and
fixture delays its slope is
$-2\pi(\Delta\tau_{\rm RF}+\Delta\tau_{\rm IF}+\Delta\tau_{\rm fixture})$.
Constant LO-path phase contributes to the intercept, not this slope.
With dispersion the fit represents a local derivative of combined response.
Keeping IF fixed by retuning LO with RF instead gives ideal nondispersive

+2\pi\Delta\tau_{\rm LO}$: IF delay no longer contributes a frequency slope.

$$y_k=b_0-2\pi(f_k-f_0)\Delta\tau_{\rm eff}+\epsilon_k.$$

a&=\frac{\sum(f_k-\bar f)(y_k-\bar y)}{\sum(f_k-\bar f)^2},\\
\widehat{\Delta\tau}_{\rm eff}&=-a/(2\pi),\\
\widehat b_0&=b_{\rm mean}+a(f_0-\bar f).
\end{aligned}$$ {#eq-phase-fit}

unless they coincide. The module returns named mean-frequency, mean-phase and

6.5% and 8.5%. Matching to 2 ps/K increases the drift-only age scale to 34.72 s,
but latency and snapshot bias still apply. These bounds concern drift, not total
absolute error: standard uncertainty is not a deterministic bound. A random-walk
drift instead needs increment covariance and a probabilistic criterion.

### Constant uncertainty and time-varying updates

For frozen correction C in one valid segment, define local absolute residual
$e_a=X_a-C$, where $X_a$ is a specified phase average at use:

$$\operatorname{var}e_a=V_a+V_C-2\operatorname{cov}(X_a,C).$$ {#eq-absolute-phase}

If $C=X_{\rm cal}+\epsilon$, expand all covariances of use, calibration and
epsilon; independent epsilon does not make use and calibration independent.
Static fixture uncertainty and quantization affect absolute phase accuracy
across realizations. Independent 0.05-degree C and an instantaneous band-limited
X of 0.362364-degree SD give a **local absolute** SD of 0.365797 degree.
This is not a new selected-band SD.

For DC-rejecting phase operator B, $B(0)=0$, constant C over the analysis segment
gives $B[X-C]=BX$. For sampled weights the calibration variance contribution is
$(\sum w_k)^2V_C-2(\sum w_k)\operatorname{cov}(\sum w_kX_k,C)$, zero when
$\sum w_k=0$, even for correlated X and C. The compact band SD remains
0.362364 degree. Finite-record mean handling and edges must implement that
operator: cropping a constant to a window and Fourier transforming can leak it,
which is a different observation. Do not filter across update steps as if C
were constant.

For updates write $c(t)=\sum_n c_n p_n(t)$, where $p_n$ holds from application n
until application n+1. Residual $e(t)=X(t)-c(t)$ then has

$$R_c(t,u)=\sum_{nm}p_n(t)p_m(u)\operatorname{cov}(c_n,c_m),$$

and $R_e(t,u)=R_X(t,u)+R_c(t,u)-\operatorname{cov}(X(t),c(u))-\operatorname{cov}(c(t),X(u))$.
Use these two-time kernels with actual observation weights and invalid-data mask.
Periodic updates generally give a cyclostationary process, not a static variance
to add to a band integral. In the special model of independent zero-mean update
errors of variance $v_c$, period P, and a uniformly randomized grid origin
independent of X, $R_c(\tau)=v_c(1-|\tau|/P)_+$ and
$S_c(f)=v_cP\operatorname{sinc}^2(fP)$, the transform of that triangle.
This has nonzero power away from DC. Correlated updates/use require cross terms
where stationary spectra apply, or the two-time formulation otherwise. This
special update-error example does not model all receiver drift as stationary.

A blind correction that subtracts the measured current phase can remove the
wanted differential input phase too. Verify with an independently imposed known
phase step at P2. A calibration interval must contain a known stimulus, or an
extra observable separating wanted phase from drift. Lower displayed residual
is not sufficient evidence of improved sensing.

Translate the allocation into hardware obligations: characterize electrical
rather than geometrical matching at L1/L2, isolate LO branch loads, control return
currents and supply-to-phase sensitivity, place thermometers to resolve gradients,
restrain phase-sensitive cables and provide endpoint test access. For example,
an assumed 0.1 rad/V differential supply sensitivity and 10 mV change produce
0.001 rad, or 0.0573 degree; filtering or regulation must address the actual
aggressor spectrum and return path. The sensitivity is unverified. A uniform
chamber temperature does not establish gradient immunity.

![State sequence with an explicit invalid-data gate. Failed acquisition or checks, changed state, stale calibration and lost amplitude or reference require reacquisition and renewed evidence before wanted-data use. A held-out fit check does not independently test acquisition or instrument errors.](figures/relative-phase-state-sequence.svg){#fig-phase-states fig-alt="A sequence from reset through acquisition, resolved branch and applicable calibration, held-out model checking and independent validity evidence reaches valid use. Failure or invalidation gates data and returns to acquisition."}

Define separate cold power-up, warm reset, partial-channel reset and retune
procedures. Record divider/PLL state where accessible, mixer/gain setting,
acquisition epoch, NCO phase if used, calibration version and settling criteria.
Frequency lock alone imposes no unique phase intercept. A run-dependent unknown
constant can leave within-run increments quiet and restart repeatability poor.
Do not unwrap across a reset and classify it as continuous drift.

For N genuinely independent restarts with zero observed invalid outcomes, the
one-sided upper failure probability at confidence $1-\alpha$ is
$1-\alpha^{1/N}$: solve $(1-p)^N=\alpha$. This binomial statement requires a
specified failure event and independent representative trials; it does not prove
deterministic phase. No restart trials have occurred here.

## Measurement and uncertainty: an executable protocol {#sec-phase-measurement}

For each source/fixture/receiver assignment, a small-error equation at tone F is

$$m(F,t)=D_F*s+\delta_{\rm wanted}(F,t)+c_{\rm fix}(F,t)
 +b_R(F,t,q)-\Delta\ell(F,t,q)+a_{\rm acq}(F,t)
 +i_{\rm inst}(F,t)+\eta(F,t).$$ {#eq-measurement}

Here $D_F=K_2-K_1$ is the unequal fixture transfer of source phase s,
$c_{\rm fix}$ is deterministic/uncertain splitter and cable phase, $b_R$ is
receiver RF/conversion/IF response excluding LO, and $\Delta\ell=\ell_2-\ell_1$.
Acquisition includes channel response and the linear sample-epoch contribution
$2\pi f_{\rm IF}(\epsilon_2-\epsilon_1)$ when sampling at $t+\epsilon_i$.
Instrument/reference phase is separate; eta collects justified small additive
phase errors. None is presumed independent. Apply the specified observation
and known-stimulus correction to this equation; do not discard common terms
without propagating their unequal paths.

| Intervention (output channel labels fixed) | Identifiable contribution under stability assumptions | Remaining ambiguity |
|---|---|---|
| Exchange characterized input fixture branches, same source/state | Fixture/source-path difference reverses; fixed receiver/LO/acquisition terms do not; half-difference extracts reversible contribution | Reconnection/drift and mixed source/fixture effects; internal terms stay combined |
| Exchange acquisition analog inputs/cables at fixed Q planes | Receiver output difference at Q reverses while acquisition/instrument channel asymmetry need not | Output fixture changes, loading, common instrument error |
| Exchange whole receiver channels | Receiver/LO terms move with their hardware; recompute all assignments | No generic sign flip isolates receiver if fixtures/clock/state also move |
| Change one LO delay, heat a branch, vary level | Test predicted sign/dependence of LO, thermal or noise/AM-to-PM terms | Other sensitive paths can respond too |
| Independently acquired comparison at Q1/Q2 | $m'=\delta_Q+a'+i'+\eta'$ observes the same receiver IF-output relationship | $m-m'$ cancels $\delta_Q$, testing acquisition/instrument difference, not absolute truth; shared paths retain common bias |

1. Use fixed LO and simultaneous-comb acquisition as above. Record physical P/L/O
   planes, channelizer/NCO response, state, temperatures, levels and coefficient
   epoch. Verify all-tone headroom, antialias response and channel rejection.
2. Characterize input/output fixture phase and slope with uncertainty. Collect
   10 ms or 50 ms simultaneous calibration snapshots according to the allocation,
   gating the stated settling and update intervals. Unknown fixture slope remains
   inseparable from receiver/acquisition slope.
3. In a separate validation run, freeze coefficients and collect 100 s per-tone
   complex envelopes at 100 ksample/s. Retain complex samples, amplitudes, flags,
   wrapped phase and epoch/state metadata. Distinguish phase of averaged product
   from averaged extracted phase. Specify phase filters, edges, window/leakage
   before comparing with ideal B. Do not add static uncertainty to its band result.
4. Fit only common-state locally unwrapped phases. Apply scalar 1 GHz correction
   and evaluate held-out 1000.5 MHz/time data, curvature and independently imposed
   wanted phase steps. A synthetic line fit establishes no fixture removal or
   physical phase-state control.
5. Execute paired swaps and perturbations with stable conditions or measured
   drift correction. Preserve assignments so every term in @eq-measurement
   can be traced; changes cannot be pooled as identical repetitions.
6. Use separate acquisition at Q1/Q2 for the differently referenced comparison;
   recomputing the same O samples cannot independently test Q-to-O acquisition.
   Give the second chain its own equation, uncertainty
   and cross-covariance. Disagreement diagnoses combined error; agreement does
   not establish accuracy when important paths are shared.
7. Execute restart/retune classes separately, using the 5–5.01 s observation and
   reporting invalid events. A fixed-state delay fit does not extend across
   unknown tuning offsets. Instruments, settling and lab execution are unverified.

For uncertainty, model the measurement process including corrections, fixtures
and covariance. First-order propagation is local and may fail for wrapped or
ambiguous quantities [@taylor1994uncertainty, app. A.1–A.3]. An illustrative
locally linear **absolute phase-result** budget (not the band statistic) has two phase terms of standard uncertainty 0.03 degree,
correlation 0.8, differenced; plus independent fixture and calibration terms
0.04 and 0.02 degree. Expansion gives

$$u_c^2=2(0.03)^2(1-0.8)+(0.04)^2+(0.02)^2
 =0.00236\ {\rm degree}^2,\quad u_c=0.04858\ {\rm degree}.$$

Twice this is 0.09716 degree; it is not automatically a 95% coverage interval.
The correlation and distributions are assumed, not measured. Ignoring covariance
would give 0.06164 degree; covariance with the opposite sign would increase the
uncertainty. Unknown fixture bias cannot be dismissed because repetitions agree.
Do not subtract an apparent instrument noise floor without a supported covariance
and measurement model. Untested offsets below 1 Hz and above 10 kHz cannot be
assigned zero merely because the teaching allocation excluded them.

A borderline test requires a declared decision rule. For an illustrative scalar
upper limit L and a justified error bound U, $\hat y+U\le L$ supports guarded
acceptance under that bound; $\hat y-U>L$ supports rejection; the overlap is
inconclusive. A standard uncertainty is not a guaranteed bound, and the rule for
phase variance requires uncertainty in that estimated statistic, not the phase
intercept budget above. No real compliance decision is made here.

Before consulting the diagnostics, produce a model, calculation and evidence

- Replace the shared source with independent references of equal marginal PSD.
  Which cross terms disappear? Does equal frequency establish restart phase?
- Keep phase variance fixed but make phase constant within each observation

- Double calibration separation L while keeping the averaging duration fixed.

- Increase signal bandwidth while keeping tone correction perfect. What phase
  slope remains, and what additional measurement/correction becomes necessary?

1	# Acquisition, tracking and signal retention {#sec-tracking-retention}
     2	
     3	An estimate from a finite burst can initialize a receiver, but it cannot keep a
     4	local reference aligned indefinitely. Feedback can follow changing phase. It can
     5	also remove the physical phase variation we meant to measure. The engineering
     6	question is therefore not simply how to minimize a detector error: it is how to
     7	retain the wanted signal while controlling nuisance phase and avoiding unsupported
     8	claims about acquisition and recovery.
     9	
    10	We use the observation and phase conventions developed in
    11	[Chapters 1–3](observation-weighted-coherence.qmd), and the local/global inference
    12	distinction in [Chapter 5](phase-delay-inference.qmd). No specialist control theory
    13	is presumed. This is a scalar continuous-time teaching model of a phase tracker,
    14	not a complete receiver or a digital synchronization design. Inputs and targets
    15	are illustrative. The mathematical model and local conventions do not establish
    16	hardware performance or book-wide convention authority.
    17	
    18	## Build the loop from its physical actions
    19	
    20	Let $\theta(t)$ be incoming phase relative to a declared ideal carrier at a receiver
    21	comparison plane, and let $\widehat\theta(t)$ be the local oscillator's correction phase
    22	referred to the same orientation and epoch. Its instantaneous frequency correction
    23	is $\dot{\widehat\theta}/(2\pi)$ in Hz. A phase detector sees their difference plus a
    24	small equivalent input phase error $n(t)$. In a locked, amplitude-valid interval,
    25	normalize the detector's slope to unity and model the correction law as
    26	
    27	$$
    28	 \dot{\widehat\theta}=k(\theta+n-\widehat\theta),\qquad k>0.
    29	$$
    30	
    31	The gain $k$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$: oscillator integration converts a frequency command
    32	to phase. This is proportional feedback through an ideal oscillator. Actual detector
    33	and actuator gains must multiply to this $k$ after unit conversion. Saturation,
    34	processing delay, oscillator tuning limits, fades and wrapped detector behavior
    35	are omitted for this locked-state model. Define true residual $e=\theta-\widehat\theta$;
    36	the measured detector quantity is $e+n$, which has different noise statistics.
    37	
    38	The two output paths in @fig-tracking-loop answer different engineering questions.
    39	The true residual subtracts the oscillator phase; detector noise also enters the
    40	correction and therefore contributes with a negative sign to that residual.
    41	The noisy detector reading includes its own direct noise term.
    42	
    43	![Locked-state feedback at one comparison plane. The incoming wanted and nuisance phase share a transfer; the detector reading and true residual differ. All phase variables are radians.](figures/tracking-loop.svg){#fig-tracking-loop fig-alt="Incoming phase and detector noise drive an oscillator correction through negative feedback. The estimate contains positive filtered noise; the true residual contains its negative, while detector output adds the original noise."}
    44	
    45	With zero initial conditions, replacing differentiation by the Laplace variable $s$
    46	turns the differential equation into an algebraic equation. Solving gives
    47	
    48	$$
    49	 T(s)={k\over s+k},\qquad E(s)=1-T(s)={s\over s+k},
    50	 \quad \widehat\Theta=T(\Theta+N),\qquad e=E\theta-Tn.
    51	$$
    52	
    53	Capital symbols denote transforms; the final relation also denotes the corresponding
    54	linear filtering. A perturbation decays as $\exp(-kt)$, so this ideal closed loop is
    55	stable. It has one pole at $-k$ and time constant $1/k$. A phase step $\Delta$ gives
    56	residual $\Delta\exp(-kt)$; a constant phase rate $\Omega$ gives steady residual $\Omega/k$.
    57	These results follow by solving $\dot e+ke=\dot\theta$ with $n=0$. They describe
    58	linear tracking after initialization, not general capture of an unknown carrier.
    59	The small-error replacement of a sinusoidal detector and the separation of input
    60	phase distortion from detector noise are developed in Tausworthe's
    61	[JPL report](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19660008034/downloads/19660008034.pdf),
    62	Part I §§3-C and 5-A. We derive this specific normalization rather than importing
    63	its bandwidth or power conventions.
    64	
    65	## Trace the wanted signal before selecting bandwidth
    66	
    67	Write $\theta=\theta_s+\theta_d$, where $\theta_s$ is a wanted physical phase variation and
    68	$\theta_d$ is nuisance reference phase. If they enter the same detector input, both
    69	receive the same transfer. In the local oscillator phase estimate they pass through
    70	$T$; in the residual they pass through $E$. A loop cannot infer which part is wanted
    71	from that input alone.
    72	
    73	For a sinusoidal phase component at offset frequency $f$, substitute $s=j2\pi f$.
    74	Writing $f_c=k/(2\pi)$, the magnitudes are
    75	
    76	$$
    77	 |T|={1\over\sqrt{1+(f/f_c)^2}},\qquad
    78	 |E|={|f|/f_c\over\sqrt{1+(f/f_c)^2}}.
    79	$$
    80	
    81	Here $f_c$ is a loop corner frequency, not the RF carrier. As $f$ tends to zero, the
    82	estimate tracks and the residual suppresses the incoming variation. For a sensing
    83	phase variation at 1 Hz and $f_c=100$ Hz, residual amplitude is only 0.0099995 of
    84	its input value. Calling that quiet residual a faithful measurement would remove
    85	about 99 percent of the desired amplitude. The estimate output retains almost all
    86	of it, but also retains low-frequency nuisance phase at that input. Reconstruction
    87	by adding the estimate and true residual is an identity; the available detector
    88	residual includes $n$ and must be interpreted accordingly.
    89	
    90	This is an interface decision. A communications receiver may use tracked carrier
    91	phase to derotate a known pilot while retaining information through a separate
    92	modulation-aware path. A phase sensor may need the correction command as part of
    93	its reported observable. Simply choosing the narrowest or widest loop cannot
    94	substitute for identifying where the wanted signal enters and is read out.
    95	
    96	## Noise bandwidth and a worked tradeoff
    97	
    98	Let $n$ be a centered stationary phase error with two-sided density $S_0$ rad²/Hz on
    99	$|f|\leq B$, zero outside. Assume stable amplitude, linear phase detection and that no
   100	other loop noise is present. The true residual's detector-noise contribution is
   101	$-Tn$, and its variance is
   102	
   103	$$
   104	 v_n=\int_{-B}^{B} S_0 {k^2\over k^2+(2\pi f)^2}\,df
   105	 ={S_0k\over\pi}\tan^{-1}\left({2\pi B\over k}\right).
   106	$$
   107	
   108	The integral is evaluated by substituting $u=2\pi f/k$. For $B$ much larger than $f_c$,
   109	$v_n$ approaches $S_0k/2$. A locally defined one-sided equivalent noise bandwidth is
   110	$\int_0^\infty|T(j2\pi f)|^2df=k/4$; the two-sided integral is $k/2$. These
   111	are explicit definitions in Hz, not a universal imported PLL bandwidth convention.
   112	White phase noise over an infinite band is an idealized limiting model; the finite
   113	$B$ formulation keeps the observation bandwidth explicit.
   114	
   115	Suppose a residual frequency offset of 0.5 Hz remains after coarse acquisition,
   116	so $\Omega=\pi$ rad/s. Let $S_0=10^{-6}$ rad²/Hz and $B=1000$ Hz. The following long-time,
   117	locked-state values exclude initial transients:
   118	
   119	| Loop corner | Noise RMS | Steady phase bias | Root mean-square true residual |
   120	|---|---:|---:|---:|
   121	| 10 Hz | 0.00558712 rad | 0.050000 rad | 0.0503112 rad |
   122	| 100 Hz | 0.0171530 rad | 0.005000 rad | 0.0178669 rad |
   123	
   124	The last column is $\sqrt{v_n+(\Omega/k)^2}$, since centered noise adds variance to
   125	the deterministic squared bias. An illustrative 0.02 rad total-RMS target rejects
   126	the narrower loop and admits the wider one under this model. However, the wider
   127	loop strongly suppresses a 1 Hz wanted variation at the residual output. The
   128	receiver decision must consider both error and wanted transfer. Hardware delay,
   129	oscillator noise and saturation could change the feasible choice; none is
   130	validated by this calculation.

   132	The upper panel of @fig-tracking-transfer-budget shows why a small residual may

## Calibration, drift and implementation {#sec-phase-calibration}

Use a **fixed 990 MHz LO** throughout each calibration cycle. Inject a simultaneous
coherent comb at 999, 1000 and 1001.5 MHz; reserve 1000.5 MHz for a held-out test.
Both channels acquire complex I/Q at 32 Msample/s with an analog/complex passband
covering IF 9–11.5 MHz plus sidebands. Per-tone DDCs use identical frequencies
and common sample-index phase origins in both channels. Each channelizer must
suppress other tones before decimation to 100 ksample/s, with passband flat over
the 10 kHz phase sidebands. The total comb level must remain linear. These
100 ksample/s streams carry narrowband envelopes, not unchannelized MHz-spaced
tones. No LO retuning, NCO reset or gain-state change occurs between training
frequencies. Hardware meeting this interface is assumed, not verified.

The measured phase is referred from Pi to the selected Oi channelizer output,
including IF/acquisition response unless de-embedded. At fixed LO an RF sweep
changes IF by the same increment. For nondispersive differential RF, IF and
fixture delays its slope is
$-2\pi(\Delta\tau_{\rm RF}+\Delta\tau_{\rm IF}+\Delta\tau_{\rm fixture})$.
Constant LO-path phase contributes to the intercept, not this slope.
With dispersion the fit represents a local derivative of combined response.
Keeping IF fixed by retuning LO with RF instead gives ideal nondispersive
slope $-2\pi(\Delta\tau_{\rm RF}+\Delta\tau_{\rm fixture})
+2\pi\Delta\tau_{\rm LO}$: IF delay no longer contributes a frequency slope.
Frequency-dependent conversion response and tuning-state offsets need their own
terms. Independent unknown offsets at each tune make a delay fit unidentifiable.
Fixture slope is indistinguishable from receiver slope unless characterized.

Let $y_k=m(f_k)-\widehat c_{\rm fixture}(f_k)$, retaining correction uncertainty,
and define the intercept $b_0$ at the stated reference $f_0=1$ GHz:

$$y_k=b_0-2\pi(f_k-f_0)\Delta\tau_{\rm eff}+\epsilon_k.$$

For locally unwrapped equal-variance observations with zero cross-covariance,
minimize $\sum[y_k-b_{\rm mean}-a(f_k-\bar f)]^2$. Differentiation gives

$$\begin{aligned}
b_{\rm mean}&=\bar y,\\
a&=\frac{\sum(f_k-\bar f)(y_k-\bar y)}{\sum(f_k-\bar f)^2},\\
\widehat{\Delta\tau}_{\rm eff}&=-a/(2\pi),\\
\widehat b_0&=b_{\rm mean}+a(f_0-\bar f).
\end{aligned}$$ {#eq-phase-fit}

The intercept at the measurement mean frequency is **not** the intercept at f0
unless they coincide. The module returns named mean-frequency, mean-phase and
delay fields; its phase_at(f0) method performs the conversion. For asymmetric
999, 1000, 1001.5 MHz synthetic data with $b_0=0.3$ rad and delay 2 ns,
$\bar f=1000.1666667$ MHz and $b_{\rm mean}=0.2979056$ rad, while
$\widehat b_0=0.3$ rad. Held-out prediction at 1000.5 MHz checks this local line,
not a demonstrated calibration algorithm. Correlated errors require covariance
weighting and an appropriate uncertainty model.

Common phase state, adequate SNR and locally resolved wrapping are prerequisites.
On this 0.5 MHz grid, delays separated by 2 microseconds can give identical wrapped
samples after an intercept change. A justified local prior (for example
$|\Delta\tau_{\rm eff}|<1$ microsecond after fixture correction), or extra frequency
information, is needed. The code rejects explicitly wrapped data and supplied
mixed/missing state IDs; it cannot detect an unreported reset or infer an unwrap.
Constant fixture phase has the same confounding freedom as fixture slope.
Hold out time, frequency and state data and inspect curvature before using the fit.

Apply scalar unit-magnitude correction at the carrier. It does not repair
wideband delay, additive noise, lost samples or clipping. A coefficient step q
rad creates at most q/2 static error, not automatically white q²/12 noise.

### Thermal reference and maintenance allocation
rather than geometrical matching at L1/L2, isolate LO branch loads, control return
currents and supply-to-phase sensitivity, place thermometers to resolve gradients,
restrain phase-sensitive cables and provide endpoint test access. For example,
an assumed 0.1 rad/V differential supply sensitivity and 10 mV change produce
0.001 rad, or 0.0573 degree; filtering or regulation must address the actual
aggressor spectrum and return path. The sensitivity is unverified. A uniform
chamber temperature does not establish gradient immunity.

Failed acquisition or checks, changed state, stale calibration and lost amplitude or reference require reacquisition and renewed evidence before wanted-data use. A held-out fit check does not independently test acquisition or instrument errors.](figures/relative-phase-state-sequence.svg){#fig-phase-states fig-alt="A sequence from reset through acquisition, resolved branch and applicable calibration, held-out model checking and independent validity evidence reaches valid use. Failure or invalidation gates data and returns to acquisition."}

Define separate cold power-up, warm reset, partial-channel reset and retune
procedures. Record divider/PLL state where accessible, mixer/gain setting,
acquisition epoch, NCO phase if used, calibration version and settling criteria.
Frequency lock alone imposes no unique phase intercept. A run-dependent unknown
constant can leave within-run increments quiet and restart repeatability poor.
Do not unwrap across a reset and classify it as continuous drift.

For N genuinely independent restarts with zero observed invalid outcomes, the
one-sided upper failure probability at confidence $1-\alpha$ is
$1-\alpha^{1/N}$: solve $(1-p)^N=\alpha$. This binomial statement requires a
specified failure event and independent representative trials; it does not prove
deterministic phase. No restart trials have occurred here.

## Measurement and uncertainty: an executable protocol {#sec-phase-measurement}

For each source/fixture/receiver assignment, a small-error equation at tone F is

$$m(F,t)=D_F*s+\delta_{\rm wanted}(F,t)+c_{\rm fix}(F,t)
 +b_R(F,t,q)-\Delta\ell(F,t,q)+a_{\rm acq}(F,t)
 +i_{\rm inst}(F,t)+\eta(F,t).$$ {#eq-measurement}

Here $D_F=K_2-K_1$ is the unequal fixture transfer of source phase s,
$c_{\rm fix}$ is deterministic/uncertain splitter and cable phase, $b_R$ is
receiver RF/conversion/IF response excluding LO, and $\Delta\ell=\ell_2-\ell_1$.
Acquisition includes channel response and the linear sample-epoch contribution
$2\pi f_{\rm IF}(\epsilon_2-\epsilon_1)$ when sampling at $t+\epsilon_i$.
Instrument/reference phase is separate; eta collects justified small additive
phase errors. None is presumed independent. Apply the specified observation
and known-stimulus correction to this equation; do not discard common terms
without propagating their unequal paths.

| Intervention (output channel labels fixed) | Identifiable contribution under stability assumptions | Remaining ambiguity |
|---|---|---|
| Exchange characterized input fixture branches, same source/state | Fixture/source-path difference reverses; fixed receiver/LO/acquisition terms do not; half-difference extracts reversible contribution | Reconnection/drift and mixed source/fixture effects; internal terms stay combined |
| Exchange acquisition analog inputs/cables at fixed Q planes | Receiver output difference at Q reverses while acquisition/instrument channel asymmetry need not | Output fixture changes, loading, common instrument error |
| Exchange whole receiver channels | Receiver/LO terms move with their hardware; recompute all assignments | No generic sign flip isolates receiver if fixtures/clock/state also move |
| Change one LO delay, heat a branch, vary level | Test predicted sign/dependence of LO, thermal or noise/AM-to-PM terms | Other sensitive paths can respond too |
| Independently acquired comparison at Q1/Q2 | $m'=\delta_Q+a'+i'+\eta'$ observes the same receiver IF-output relationship | $m-m'$ cancels $\delta_Q$, testing acquisition/instrument difference, not absolute truth; shared paths retain common bias |

1. Use fixed LO and simultaneous-comb acquisition as above. Record physical P/L/O
   planes, channelizer/NCO response, state, temperatures, levels and coefficient
   epoch. Verify all-tone headroom, antialias response and channel rejection.
2. Characterize input/output fixture phase and slope with uncertainty. Collect
   10 ms or 50 ms simultaneous calibration snapshots according to the allocation,
   gating the stated settling and update intervals. Unknown fixture slope remains
   inseparable from receiver/acquisition slope.
3. In a separate validation run, freeze coefficients and collect 100 s per-tone
   complex envelopes at 100 ksample/s. Retain complex samples, amplitudes, flags,
   wrapped phase and epoch/state metadata. Distinguish phase of averaged product
   from averaged extracted phase. Specify phase filters, edges, window/leakage
   before comparing with ideal B. Do not add static uncertainty to its band result.
4. Fit only common-state locally unwrapped phases. Apply scalar 1 GHz correction
   and evaluate held-out 1000.5 MHz/time data, curvature and independently imposed
   wanted phase steps. A synthetic line fit establishes no fixture removal or
   physical phase-state control.
5. Execute paired swaps and perturbations with stable conditions or measured
   drift correction. Preserve assignments so every term in @eq-measurement
   can be traced; changes cannot be pooled as identical repetitions.
6. Use separate acquisition at Q1/Q2 for the differently referenced comparison;
   recomputing the same O samples cannot independently test Q-to-O acquisition.
   Give the second chain its own equation, uncertainty
   and cross-covariance. Disagreement diagnoses combined error; agreement does
   not establish accuracy when important paths are shared.
7. Execute restart/retune classes separately, using the 5–5.01 s observation and
   reporting invalid events. A fixed-state delay fit does not extend across
   unknown tuning offsets. Instruments, settling and lab execution are unverified.

For uncertainty, model the measurement process including corrections, fixtures
and covariance. First-order propagation is local and may fail for wrapped or
ambiguous quantities [@taylor1994uncertainty, app. A.1–A.3]. An illustrative
locally linear **absolute phase-result** budget (not the band statistic) has two phase terms of standard uncertainty 0.03 degree,
correlation 0.8, differenced; plus independent fixture and calibration terms
0.04 and 0.02 degree. Expansion gives

$$u_c^2=2(0.03)^2(1-0.8)+(0.04)^2+(0.02)^2
 =0.00236\ {\rm degree}^2,\quad u_c=0.04858\ {\rm degree}.$$

Twice this is 0.09716 degree; it is not automatically a 95% coverage interval.
The correlation and distributions are assumed, not measured. Ignoring covariance
would give 0.06164 degree; covariance with the opposite sign would increase the
uncertainty. Unknown fixture bias cannot be dismissed because repetitions agree.
Do not subtract an apparent instrument noise floor without a supported covariance
and measurement model. Untested offsets below 1 Hz and above 10 kHz cannot be
assigned zero merely because the teaching allocation excluded them.

A borderline test requires a declared decision rule. For an illustrative scalar
upper limit L and a justified error bound U, $\hat y+U\le L$ supports guarded
acceptance under that bound; $\hat y-U>L$ supports rejection; the overlap is
inconclusive. A standard uncertainty is not a guaranteed bound, and the rule for
phase variance requires uncertainty in that estimated statistic, not the phase
intercept budget above. No real compliance decision is made here.
